title: North Atlantic right whales no match for vessel strikes, entanglements between Canada and U.S.
summary: With the latest estimates putting the North Atlantic right whale population at just 382, a consortium is calling for urgent action to safeguard the species' survival.

image.caption: Silt and her sixth known calf, seen off Anticosti Island, Que. in September 2026. Twenty four new North Atlantic right whales were born this year. (Submitted by Mingan Island Cetacean Study)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador
With the latest estimates putting the North Atlantic right whale population at just 382, a consortium is calling for urgent action to safeguard the species' survival.
Recovery depends on sustained protective action in both countries, says Heather Pettis

Although 2026 marked a record high for North Atlantic right whale births since 2009 — with 24 calves documented, including a newborn seen with its mother Silt off the coast of Quebec in September — these newborn whales remain vulnerable to ongoing fatal threats.
With the latest estimates putting the population at just 382, the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium is calling for urgent action to safeguard the species' survival.

“The newly released right whale population estimate underscores that more work is needed to protect this species," said Heather Pettis, who leads the right whale research program in the Anderson Cabot Center and chairs the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium.
"The population is not yet on a clear path to recovery and is incredibly vulnerable to entanglements and vessel strikes — threats we know how to reduce."

On Jan. 27, a four-year-old male named “Division” was discovered off North Carolina after succumbing to severe entanglement linked to Canadian snow crab equipment. In February, researchers identified a three-year-old female found dead along a barrier island off Virginia’s eastern shore. (Submitted by Clearwater Marine Aquarium Research Institute)

Two whale mortalities have been documented in 2026. One was caused by entanglement and another from an undetermined cause. In January, the body of a whale named Division was spotted off the North Carolina coast.
The four-year-old male was first spotted in 2025 with a fishing line wrapped around his head and mouth, cutting into his blowhole and embedded in his jaw.

Less than two weeks later, the New England Aquarium identified a dead three-year-old female right whale off of Virginia. On top of the deaths, there have been eight documented cases of human-caused injuries to right whales this year: seven entanglements and one vessel strike.

Philip Hamilton, of the New England Aquarium in Boston, has been researching North Atlantic right whales since the 1980s — a passion that sprung from compassion for the sea mammals who have been on the brink of extinction for decades.
Hamilton said it’s hard to think about what a whale feels when it’s entangled in fishing gear.
“Imagine if you were wrapped in rope that moved as you moved … literally sawing into your body," he said. "It is really painful. They don’t have arms. The pain is … kind of unimaginable.”
Hamilton can call many of the remaining North Atlantic right whales by name, but the iconic Admiral has a special place in his heart.
Admiral is a favourite among biologists because of her playful surfacing. She suffered a severe entanglement in 2007, and hasn’t been seen since. (Submitted by New England Aquarium)

"She was an adult when she was first seen in 1980. She felt like the grand dame of the population. She was so big that I could tell who she was if she surfaced a mile away from the boat because she would rocket up like a submarine and bounce on the surface," Hamilton said.
"She was known to do headstands in certain habitats, so you'd just see her with her tail sticking up in the air."
But the iconic Admiral hasn’t been seen in over a decade after a bad entanglement with fishing lines.
“The right whales are doing their part. We need to make sure we are doing our part to protect them, because they can’t do anything more than what they’re doing,” Hamilton said.
Whale-safe gear
In February, Ottawa launched a Whale-safe Gear Strategy. They’ve been testing ropeless fishing gear in eastern Canada since, including in western Newfoundland.
Andrea Morden, who works with DFO whale management, said by working with fishers, they’ve made progress in entanglement reduction and in showing what a future whale-safe fishery could look like.
Right whales set record high for births in 2026, but conservation group says species still vulnerable and protection is needed
“What we have learned is that it’s not going to be a one-size-fits-all gear solution that works across the diversity of eastern Canadian fisheries,” she said.

Morden said some fisheries are higher-risk, like crab and lobster, because of their extensive use of rope. She said DFO is collaborating with the fishing industry to test gear adaptations that support both economic prosperity and the recovery of the North Atlantic right whale population.
It’s not just ropeless gear, but adaptations that are less likely to entangle a whale, including lower breaking-strength rope and on-demand fishing gear that works remotely.
Whale aware

Smiling ear to ear, Newfoundland-based marine mammal scientist Jack Lawson said Newfoundlanders and Labradorians are fortunate to witness the ocean, including sightings of a North Atlantic right whale earlier this summer. But Lawson said that proximity to nature comes with responsibility.

“We have the benefit of all these animals coming to our waters every year, and I think we have the responsibility as well to be careful around them,” said Lawson, who studies the North Atlantic right whale.
Jack Lawson says it’s exciting to see North Atlantic right whales in Newfoundland and Labrador waters. But he fears for their safety as they get closer to coastlines. (Leila Beaudoin/CBC)
He said it's not just about policy but awareness — from small boats to large ships — that these mammals may be nearby and a strike could be fatal.

blocks.text: Scientists say predicting where North Atlantic right whale collisions will occur is difficult. The species' movement is heavily influenced by seasonal migration and calving needs, which is why researchers are calling for stronger collaboration between Canada and the United States.
Pettis said recovery for the species depends on sustained protective action in both countries.
